title: Staying when it's hard
hookLine: churches disappoint; staying can be faithful, and so, sometimes, can leaving well
tomorrow: the food pantry needs hands saturday. who signs up first?

cards: Car keys in your hand, engine off, the church parking lot after a service that stung. Maybe the choir just split over a fight. Maybe a leader let people down.
The keys feel heavier than they are, because they're the question: stay, or go? The New Testament speaks to that moment, because its churches had trouble too.

teach.b: Take Corinth. Paul opens his first letter there with bad news: “it hath been declared unto me of you, my brethren, by them which are of the house of Chloe, that there are contentions among you.”
Quarrels, factions, people lining up behind favorite leaders. Yet a few lines earlier he greets them as “the church of God which is at Corinth.”
Messy, and still the church of God. Paul names the trouble honestly and writes to them instead of writing them off.

The letter to the Hebrews speaks to people tempted to drift: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another.” But the New Testament also tells of a parting.
Paul and Barnabas disagree over taking Mark along, and Acts says “the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other.” Both kept serving.
Later, in the second letter to Timothy, Paul asks for Mark by name: he is “profitable to me for the ministry.”
So staying can be faithful, and sometimes leaving well is faithful too: honestly, without slander, still wishing the others good. Churches teach different things about when to move on.
One thing comes first for everyone: if someone has been harmed at church, getting safe is not a failure of faith.

how: Christians disappointed by a church may pray about it, talk with a pastor or a trusted friend, and weigh staying or leaving; churches differ in what they teach about moving on.

games.q: what does “staying when it's hard” mean?
o: attending out of habit after belief is gone
keeping faith with a church through disappointment
putting up with harm because leaving is a sin

games.q: trouble in the early churches — tap the pairs.
p: Mark, in the letter to Timothy

s: Paul refused to call the quarreling Corinthians a church
he greets them as the church of God which is at Corinth.
Hebrews says some were already drifting from the gatherings
not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is.
after their split, Paul and Barnabas both stopped serving
Barnabas took Mark to Cyprus; Paul chose Silas and set out.

games.q: a friend's church leader was caught lying, and she asks if leaving would mean she's lost her faith. what fits today's lesson?
o: leaving well can be faithful; if she's been harmed, getting safe comes first.
faithful people never leave a church, whatever happens there.
leave, and tell everyone exactly how awful they all are.
games.why: Paul and Barnabas parted, and both kept serving. leaving honestly, without slander, can be faithful, and getting safe from harm is never a failure of faith.

practice: Hold your keys, or any small thing you carry out the door, in your open hand, and look at it. Bring your church to mind as it really is, the good and the hard; if you have none now, one you left or wonder about.
If you pray, tell God the truth about it, and ask what faithful looks like from here.

wordCard.voice: Staying when it's hard. Keeping faith with a church through disappointment, honestly, knowing that sometimes leaving well is faithful too.

orig.note: the Greek word behind 'the assembling of ourselves together' in Hebrews 10:25.

carryVoice: Your line: faithful, honestly. Paul named the quarrels and still called them the church of God. Take care.
